Lessons.Title: Inequivalent Equations
ExplanationParagraphs: Source-aligned goals: Explain why squaring each side of an equation, or taking the square root of each side, may result in an inequivalent equation. Use graphs to represent solutions to equations involving squares and square roots.
After isolating a nonnegative square root, squaring the equation may introduce extraneous solutions. Check all candidates in the original equation.
Source activity 7.1: 2 and -2: What do you notice? What do you wonder? Explain the mathematical model, verify the relevant result and have a teacher inspect original diagrams or discussion evidence.

Source activity 7.2: Careful When You Take the Square Root: Tyler was solving this equation: \(\displaystyle x^2 - 1 = 3\) He said, “I can add 1 to each side of the equation and it doesn’t change the equation. I get \(x^2 = 4\).” How can you see the solution to the equation \(x^2 - 1 = 3\) in Figure A? How can you see the solution to the equation \(x^2 = 4\) in Figure B? Use the graphs to explain why the equations have the same… Explain the mathematical model, verify the relevant result and have a teacher inspect original diagrams or discussion evidence.

Source activity 7.3: Another Way to Solve: Han was solving this equation: \(\displaystyle \dfrac{x+3}{2} = 4\) He said, "I know that half of \(x+3\) is 4. So \(x+3\) must be 8, since half of 8 is 4. This means that \(x\) is 5." Use Han's reasoning to solve this equation: \((x+3)^2 = 4\). What advice would you give to someone who was going to solve an equation like \((x+3)^2 = 4\)? Explain the mathematical model, verify the relevant result and have a teacher inspect original diagrams or discussion evidence.

Source activity 7.4: What Happens When You Square Each Side?: Mai was solving this equation: \(\displaystyle \sqrt{x-1} = 3\) She said, “I can square each side of the equation to get another equation with the same solutions.” Then she wrote: \(\begin{align}\sqrt{x-1} &= 3\\ (\sqrt{x-1})^2 &= 3^2 \\ x-1 &= 9 \\ x &= 10 \end{align}\) Check to see if her solution makes the original equation true. Andre said, “I tried your technique to solve… Explain the mathematical model, verify the relevant result and have a teacher inspect original diagrams or discussion evidence.

Source activity 7.5: Solve These Equations With Square Roots in Them: Find the solution(s) to each of these equations, or explain why there is no solution. \(\sqrt{t + 4} = 3\) \(\text{-}10 = \text{-}\sqrt{a}\) \(\sqrt{3 - w} - 4 = 0\) \(\sqrt{z} + 9 = 0\) Are there values of \(a\) and \(b\) so that the equation \(\sqrt{t + a} = b\) has more than one solution? Explain your reasoning. Every positive number has two square roots. You can see this… Explain the mathematical model, verify the relevant result and have a teacher inspect original diagrams or discussion evidence.

Practice Problem 1: Noah solved the equation \(5x^2=45\). Here are his steps: \(\begin{align} 5x^2 &= 45 \\ x^2 &= 9 \\ x &= 3 \\ \end{align}\) Do you agree with Noah? Explain your reasoning. Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.

Practice Problem 2: Find the solution(s) to each equation, or explain why there is no solution. \(\sqrt{47-x}-2 = 4\) \(\frac12 \sqrt{20+x} = 5\) Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.
Practice Problem 3: Which is a solution to the equation \(\sqrt{5-x}+13=4\)? The equation has no solution. Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.

Practice Problem 4: Select all expressions that are equal to \(\frac{1}{(\sqrt2)^5}\). \(\text- \frac{5}{\sqrt2}\) \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^5}}\) \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{32}}\) \(\text- (\sqrt2)^5\) \(\text- 2^{\frac52}\) \(2^{\text- \frac52}\) Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.
Practice Problem 5: Which are the solutions to the equation \(x^2=36\)? This equation has no solutions. Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.

Practice Problem 6: Here is a graph of \(y=x^2\). Use the graph to estimate all solutions to the equation \(x^2=3\). If you square your estimates, what number should they be close to? Square your estimates. How close did you get to this number? Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.

Practice Problem 7: The polynomial function \(q(x)=3x^3+11x^2-14x-40\) has a known factor of \((3x + 5)\). Rewrite \(q(x)\) as the product of linear factors. Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.
Edulytics independent cool-down: Solve sqrt(x+6)=x. Expected reasoning or answer: x=3; reject -2.
